transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what's been troubling you or what brings you in today?

Well, doctor, it’s... it's a bit of a complex situation, to be perfectly honest. I’m here mostly because things at home have gotten incredibly tense, and I just need someone to look at this objectively. You see, I’m a teaching assistant—I'm finishing up my graduate degree right now—so I’m very used to analyzing texts, looking for subtext, and paying attention to details that other people might just gloss over. 

And for the past year, going back to roughly the start of last fall's term, things have been happening with my wife. I know she says the late meetings and the little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff. She tells me it's just end-of-quarter reports or administrative restructuring, and sure, on the surface, that sounds plausible. I understand how offices work. But when you actually look at it... I mean, I’ve been paying very close attention, and for the past year they’ve lined up too precisely to feel accidental. 

The specific times she texts, the sudden shifts in her punctuation, the exact phrasing she uses when she claims she's stuck at the office—it's not random. It's like there’s a private signal in them, some kind of underlying code meant to tell me something she won’t say directly. I've tried to bring it up, to show her how these anomalies correlate and point to a specific message, but she just gets defensive and acts like I'm overthinking it. But you don't just accidentally create a pattern like that, you know? There's a deliberate structure to it, and I just can't figure out why she won't just come out and say whatever it is she's trying to signal to me through all these little changes.
Do you believe that your wife is intentionally sending you hidden messages through her texts and behavior, and if so, how do you know this is happening despite her saying it’s just work-related?

Yes, exactly. I mean, I know I just touched on this, but it really is the absolute center of the whole issue. When I ask her about it, I know my wife says the late meetings and the little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff. She’ll wave it off and say, 'Oh, it’s just the quarterly reports,' or 'We're doing administrative restructuring again.' And, you know, I want to be a reasonable husband. I listen to her. I try to take it at face value. 

But then I actually sit down and look at the timeline of events. If it were just one late meeting, or if she just suddenly started using periods at the end of texts where she used to use exclamation points, I wouldn't think twice. I'm 48 years old, I've been around long enough to know that people just get busy or tired. 

But for the past year—specifically going back to the second week of September last year, right around the 12th or 13th—these things have lined up too precisely to feel accidental. It’s the convergence of it all. It’s the way a text saying 'Running 15 mins late' always perfectly coincides with a very specific, rigid shift in her vocabulary, usually on Thursday evenings. It’s like there’s a private signal in them. It really feels like it’s meant to tell me something she won’t say directly to my face. Maybe she feels she can't say it out loud, or maybe she's testing my ability to read between the lines, knowing my background in text analysis. But the probability of these specific phrasing shifts and timing alignments happening purely by chance, week after week, month after month for an entire year... it's just statistically impossible. You don't get that kind of structural precision by accident. So yes, despite her insisting it's just work, the evidence is right there in the patterns. I just... I need to figure out what the message actually is.

Do you believe your wife’s behavior is specifically directed at you with a hidden meaning that only you are meant to understand, and do you feel that others wouldn't interpret her actions the same way you do?

Well, yes, exactly. That’s precisely it. If I were to take my phone and show these message threads to, say, my brother, or one of our mutual friends, they wouldn’t see it. They’d look at a text that says, you know, "Stuck in a review, be home by 7," and they’d just think she’s stuck in a review. Because they don't have the baseline. They don't know her textual rhythms the way I do, and they certainly don't have my background in structural analysis. So to them, sure, it looks exactly like what she claims it is. 

Like I was saying earlier, I know my wife says the late meetings and all these little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff—and that cover story works perfectly on everyone else. But she knows *I’m* the one reading them. She knows I’m the one waiting at home, paying attention. 

For the past year, these anomalies have lined up entirely too precisely to feel accidental to someone who actually knows how to look at the data. It is absolutely a private signal. It’s like she’s broadcasting on a frequency that she knows only my receiver is tuned to. She’s using the mundane details of her day to construct this... this subtext, meant to tell me something she won’t say directly. Why she won't just say it over dinner, I don't know. Maybe she's afraid of a confrontation, or maybe this is some sort of elaborate test of our connection, to see if I'm really paying attention to her. But she knows I'll catch the discrepancies. She knows I'll see the pattern. 

It's just incredibly isolating when you're the only one who can see the code, and the person writing it refuses to hand over the cipher. If I try to explain the methodology of how I found the pattern to anyone else, their eyes just glaze over because they don't want to do the work of actually analyzing the texts. I mean, you can see how that would be immensely frustrating, right? Because the intent is so clearly directed at me, and yet I'm left having to decode it all by myself while she pretends it's just administrative restructuring.
Do you believe that your wife’s behavior and messages contain a hidden meaning or code that you are uniquely able to detect, even though others may not interpret them the same way?

Yes, doctor, that is exactly what I've been trying to explain. I mean, I know it feels like we're circling the exact same point here, but it really is the crux of the whole situation, and it's so important that you understand the mechanics of it. 

I know my wife says the late meetings and all those little, granular changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff. She leans on that excuse constantly—the new administrative software, the end-of-quarter reviews, the restructuring. And if you just glance at it, sure, it looks like the standard corporate grind. But when you actually live with the person, when you study their communication habits the way I do, you see the cracks in that story. 

For the past year, all of these so-called normal occurrences have lined up way, way too precisely to feel accidental. You can't have a coincidence happen on a rigid schedule for fifty-two weeks straight. It just defies logic. It is, without a doubt, a private signal. It’s like she’s burying a secret frequency underneath the static of her daily routine, specifically meant to tell me something she just won’t say directly. 

And that is what is so maddening about all this! I'll be sitting at my desk, trying to grade undergraduate essays—which is exhausting enough on its own, let me tell you—and my phone will buzz. And it’ll be a text from her saying, "Grabbing takeout, late." But why a comma instead of her usual dash? Why "takeout" instead of "dinner," which is the noun she's used for the entirety of our marriage? To anyone else, it's nothing. But to me, the one person who knows her baseline, it screams that there's an intentional subtext. She knows I have the analytical training to detect these anomalies. She knows I'll see the code. I just... I spend hours trying to map it all out, trying to decode what she’s too afraid or too stubborn to just say to my face. I just don't understand why she insists on communicating through this elaborate puzzle instead of just talking to me like a normal person.
Do you believe your wife is trying to manipulate or control you through these messages, or do you think she's trying to communicate something else?

Manipulate? No, no, I wouldn't use the word manipulate. Control implies a sort of... well, it implies a malice or a desire for power over me that I really don't think is at play here. I don't think she's trying to make me a puppet or force me into doing something against my will. It's really more about... well, exactly what I've been trying to hammer home this whole time. 

I know I keep coming back to the same point, and I apologize if it feels redundant, but it's just so crucial to understand the distinction between manipulation and what's actually happening. Like I've been saying, I know my wife says the late meetings and those little, highly specific changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff. She swears up and down it's just the daily corporate grind. But for the past year, all of these elements have lined up far, far too precisely to feel accidental. You just don't get that level of structural consistency by chance. 

So, if it's not a control tactic, what is it? I truly believe it's a private signal. It’s... it's her way of putting something out there, meant to tell me something she simply won’t say directly to my face. People are terrified of direct vulnerability, doctor. I see it all the time in my work. When I'm grading essays for my classes, I see students bury their actual thesis under layers of passive voice and jargon because they aren't confident enough to just state their point. I think my wife is doing the exact same thing with our marriage. 

She's burying her message in the syntax of her daily routine. It's not about controlling me; it's about her inability to just sit down at the kitchen table, look me in the eye, and say whatever it is she's actually feeling. Maybe she's unhappy, maybe she wants a change, I don't know yet. But she's relying on me to read the signal because she knows I have the analytical mind to catch it. She's communicating the only way she feels safe doing so. I just... I just have to keep working at the timeline until I translate exactly what that message is.
Can you tell me what you believe the hidden message or overall meaning is that your wife is trying to communicate to you through these signals?

Well, that is... I mean, that’s the million-dollar question, isn’t it? If I knew the exact, definitive meaning of what she was trying to say, I wouldn't be spending half my week mapping out her punctuation habits and cross-referencing them with her meeting schedules. 

You see, the problem with this kind of structural analysis—and I actually tell my undergrads this all the time when we’re deconstructing modernist literature—is that identifying the presence of a cipher is really only the very first step. It’s actually the easiest part of the whole process. You spot the anomaly, you track the frequency of the deviation, you establish the baseline, and boom, you know a code exists. I’ve done all that. I have literal spreadsheets full of that data. But translating the actual semantic meaning? The core message? That requires a key. 

And the frustrating reality is that she hasn't given me the key. So I’m left looking at these fragmented signals... a delayed meeting on a Tuesday, a sudden shift to passive voice in a text about picking up the dry cleaning, the use of a period instead of an exclamation point... and I know, I absolutely know they form a cohesive narrative, but the central thesis is still entirely obscured to me. It’s like having all the pieces of a thousand-piece puzzle but someone threw away the box with the picture on it. 

I’ve hypothesized, of course. I mean, human nature dictates that I try to fill in the blanks. Is she unhappy with where we are? Is she testing my commitment, waiting to see if I care enough to figure it out? Is there some external pressure she’s facing that she feels she can’t articulate because of our current financial dynamic, what with me still being a teaching assistant at forty-eight? I just... I honestly don't know yet. I haven't cracked the core message. I just know that the architecture of a message is undeniably there, woven into the everyday static. It’s incredibly dense, exhausting work, doctor, but I can’t just ignore it when the data is screaming at me that she’s trying to say something important. I just... I need more time to compile the syntax before the actual meaning reveals itself.

Have you ever experienced any strange sensations, thoughts, or perceptions—like hearing voices, seeing things that others don’t, or believing that something is influencing your thoughts or actions in a way that others don't seem to notice?

Voices? No, no, absolutely not. I think... I think we need to be very, very clear about the distinction between what I'm describing to you and the kind of phenomena you're asking about right now. I don't hear voices, I don't see things that aren't there, and I certainly don't believe there's some sort of external force or, I don't know, a radio wave or whatever influencing my actions. 

My thoughts are entirely my own. In fact, my thoughts are probably the only thing I have complete, absolute control over right now, which is exactly why I rely on them so heavily to do this analytical work. You see, when you spend your days in academia, especially in the humanities, you learn to rely strictly on the tangible text. You don't just invent a theme because a voice in your head told you it was there; you have to cite your sources. You point to the paragraph, the sentence, the specific word choice. 

And that is exactly what I'm doing with my wife's messages. It's all tangible, empirical evidence. I'm not pulling things out of thin air or listening to whispers in the walls. I'm looking at a comma. A real, physical comma on a digital screen. If I were hearing voices, well, frankly, that would make things a lot easier, wouldn't it? Because then someone would just be handing me the answer! But no, it's just me, my own completely rational, autonomous mind, sitting in my study, looking at the data. 

I know sometimes people who are highly stressed—and I am under an immense amount of stress, let me be clear, because grading fifty freshman composition papers on a Sunday while trying to decode your marriage is an absolute nightmare—but I know stressed people might start to imagine things. My perceptions, however, are incredibly grounded. Almost painfully grounded. I notice the things that are actually, physically there that everyone else just breezes past because they aren't paying attention. So, no, no strange sensations, no hallucinations, no outside influences controlling my brain. Just a very, very heavy cognitive load from trying to process reality as it actually exists in front of me.
Do you ever feel that things in your environment, like objects, events, or other people’s actions, have a special or hidden meaning that is specifically directed at you?

Well, yes, but... I mean, I wouldn't call it a "hidden meaning" in the sense of, like, a mystical sign from the universe or something directed at me by strangers on the street. I'm not walking down the sidewalk thinking the color of a passing car is a message from God. That's... that's not what this is. It's highly specific to my immediate environment, specifically my marriage. 

It’s exactly what I’ve been trying to articulate regarding my wife. It’s not that random objects have meaning; it’s that her actions, her specific, documented actions, have a meaning directed at me that she is obscuring. Like I said before, I know she claims that these late meetings—the ones that suddenly started happening every other Thursday at 5:30 PM, right when we used to have dinner—and the little, minute changes in her text messages, like using "okay" instead of "ok," or the sudden absence of emojis when she texts about her commute... I know she says it's just normal office stuff. She says she's just busy, or tired, or whatever the convenient excuse of the day is. 

But for the past year, doctor, an entire year, they’ve lined up too precisely. You don't have a 43% increase in passive-aggressive punctuation on days when she also claims to have a "budget review" by mere coincidence. The statistical probability of that happening accidentally is astronomical. It doesn't feel accidental because it isn't accidental. It’s a private signal. It is a very deliberate, albeit heavily coded, signal meant to tell me something she won’t say directly to my face. 

And that's the part that is so exhausting. It's directed at me, yes, but it's directed at me as a puzzle to be solved, rather than a conversation to be had. She knows I'm an academic. She knows I analyze texts for a living. So she's turning our daily interactions into a text for me to analyze, because she's too afraid of the vulnerability required to just tell me what's wrong. So, yes, there is a meaning, and yes, it is directed at me, but it's not some grand delusion about the world at large; it's a very specific, very real breakdown in communication within my own home that I am desperately trying to translate.
Have you ever had beliefs or ideas that others have told you are not true or realistic, even though you felt certain they were at the time?

Well, yes, of course. I mean, we just touched on this, didn't we? This is exactly the crux of the issue with my wife. It's precisely what I've been trying to explain. 

When I try to bring this up to her—and I do, I try to approach it very logically, very calmly, usually on a weekend when the house is quiet and I can actually lay out the timeline for her—she completely dismisses it. She tells me that I'm entirely off base, that my theories are completely unrealistic. I'll sit there, and I'll say, "Look, here are the late meetings, here are the little changes in your work messages, the sudden shift in your tone on these specific dates," and she just... she shakes her head. She gets defensive, or sometimes she just sighs like I'm being ridiculous. 

I know she says it's all just normal office stuff. She tells me, "I'm just busy," or "It's just a coincidence," or she'll say I'm letting my academic work bleed into my personal life and that I'm over-analyzing a simple text about picking up milk. She insists that my belief about this is just completely untrue.

But the thing is, doctor—and this is what is so incredibly isolating about this whole experience—I know what she's saying, and I know maybe to a layman who hasn't actually looked at the data, it might sound like a stretch. But I feel completely, one-hundred-percent certain. I am certain because, for the past year, as I've been meticulously tracking this, these occurrences have lined up far too precisely to feel accidental. You simply cannot have an entire year of consistent, perfectly timed anomalies and call it a coincidence. The mathematics of it just don't allow for that. 

It's a private signal. It just is. I know in my bones that there is a private signal in them meant to tell me something she won’t say directly. And the fact that she denies it, the fact that she looks me in the eye and tells me my ideas aren't true... well, honestly, I've come to realize that her denial is likely just another layer of the obfuscation. It's a defense mechanism on her part because she's not ready to confront the actual subtext of our marriage. So, yes, she tells me I'm wrong all the time. She tells me it's not realistic. But the evidence... the empirical evidence simply doesn't support her denial.

Have you ever experienced a period of time when you felt unusually energetic, unusually confident, or unusually irritable, where you were doing more things than usual or felt like you didn't need as much sleep?

Unusually energetic? Oh, Lord, no. No, no, no. I mean, I wish I had a surplus of energy, frankly. I’m forty-eight years old, I’m a teaching assistant in a department full of twenty-three-year-old grad students who seem to survive on iced coffee and sheer willpower, and I can assure you, I am constantly exhausted. There is no unusual energy here. If anything, I am running on fumes most days. 

And as for not needing sleep... well, I think we need to separate not *getting* sleep from not *needing* sleep. Because I absolutely need it. My brain needs it to function, to do the analytical heavy lifting I was just telling you about. Do I stay up late? Yes, sometimes I'm up until two or three in the morning, but that’s not because I’m bouncing off the walls or feeling invincible. It’s because I’m sitting at the dining room table, cross-referencing my wife’s text timestamps with her supposed work schedule, or I’m trying to get through a stack of midterms on post-modern literature that I should have finished three days ago. So I’m awake, yes, but I’m miserable about it. I’m drinking chamomile tea and rubbing my temples, not... not trying to conquer the world. I desperately crave a solid eight hours.

And confident? No, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, how confident can a person really feel when the person they share their life with is constantly telling them that their reality is false? It’s profoundly destabilizing. It chips away at your confidence, actually. I'm second-guessing how to approach her, how to present the data without her shutting down. 

Now, irritable... sure, I get irritable. But you have to look at the context, doctor. I wouldn't call it an "unusual period" of irritability like it's some sort of unprovoked mood swing that just descends on me from the ether. I'm irritable because I'm exhausted, because I'm carrying a massive workload for a professor who barely knows my name, and, most importantly, because I am being subjected to a daily, agonizing psychological puzzle in my own home. Anyone would be irritable under those conditions! If someone is constantly sending you coded messages, altering their punctuation, changing their routines, and then looking you in the eye and sighing at you like you're a child when you try to discuss it... well, I'd argue that irritability is the only rational, logical response. 

But it's not a phase or a... a surge in mood. It's just the natural, proportional byproduct of my current, highly stressful environment. So, no, none of those sudden surges or bursts you're describing. Just a very, very tired man trying to keep up with his grading while making sense of his marriage.
Have you ever felt certain about something happening or being true, even though there was no solid proof and others told you it wasn't the case?

Well, I feel like we’re sort of going in circles here, Doctor, because this is exactly what we’ve been talking about. And honestly, I have to take issue with your phrasing of "no solid proof." What exactly constitutes solid proof? If you mean a signed, notarized confession from her, then no, I suppose I don't have that. But if you mean empirical data, observable behavioral patterns, linguistic anomalies... then I have an absolute abundance of proof. 

I know my wife says the late meetings and the little changes in her work messages are just normal office stuff. She tells me that constantly. She’ll look right at me and say, "I'm just busy," or "You're overthinking a simple text." And, you know, if it were just an isolated incident, if she just stayed late one Tuesday or dropped an emoji once because she was rushing to catch the train, I would absolutely concede that point. I’m a reasonable man. I understand how the world works. 

But for the past year... an entire twelve months... they’ve lined up too precisely to feel accidental. You simply cannot dismiss a year's worth of perfectly correlated data as a fluke. It defies logic. It defies basic statistical probability! So when she tells me it isn't the case, I don't see that as a lack of proof; I see it as her refusing to engage with the reality of the situation. It’s exactly like there’s a private signal in them meant to tell me something she won’t say directly. 

My certainty comes from the fact that I am the only one actually looking at the evidence objectively. I sit there at night, going over the texts, cross-referencing the meeting times, and the pattern is just glaringly obvious to anyone who would actually take the time to look at it the way I have. So, yes, I am absolutely certain, because the data doesn't lie, even if the people around you insist on ignoring it.

Have you ever felt that thoughts that aren’t yours have been placed into your mind, or that unrelated events or messages in the world around you were specifically meant for you, even if others don’t see that connection?

Thoughts placed in my mind? Oh, no, no, absolutely not. That sounds like something out of a cheap science fiction novel, frankly. My thoughts are entirely my own. I have a very rigorous, highly organized mind—it’s what makes me a good researcher, even if it does keep me up at all hours. So, no, nobody is putting thoughts into my head. 

But that second part of your question... about messages in the world being specifically meant for me... well, Doctor, I feel like a bit of a broken record here, but that is exactly what I have been trying to articulate to you this entire session! It’s like you’re finally hitting on the exact architecture of what I’m dealing with at home. 

This is precisely what I mean when I talk about her texts and her schedule. I know my wife says the late meetings and the little changes in her work messages are just "normal office stuff." She uses that exact phrase all the time, or she'll say she's just typing fast between clients. But I’ve been logging this for twelve months. And for the past year, they’ve lined up too precisely to feel accidental. 

Let me give you an example, just to illustrate how this actually manifests, because it's not just some vague feeling I have. Last Thursday, she sends a text at 4:12 PM. Not 4:15, not 4:30. 4:12. And instead of her usual, you know, "Running late, see you at 7," she writes, "Meeting ran over. Home later." The syntax is entirely truncated. No punctuation at the end. And then, I check the shared calendar, and this supposed late meeting wasn't even logged until 4:10. Do you see what I mean? The timing of the calendar update, the sudden shift in her texting style... it’s not random. A rush is random. This is designed. 

It’s like reading a text within a text—subtext, really, which is exactly what I spend my days teaching twenty-year-olds how to identify in literature. But when it's happening in your own marriage, it's exhausting. It is so clearly a private signal. There’s a private signal in those messages and schedule changes meant to tell me something she won’t say directly to my face. Maybe she wants out of the marriage but doesn't want to be the one to pull the trigger, or maybe it's something else entirely, but the message is there. It is meant for me to decode. So yes, absolutely, there are messages meant specifically for me. They're just embedded in the mundane details of her so-called "normal office stuff," and I seem to be the only one willing to look at the data and admit it.
Do you believe the hidden messages your wife is sending are harmful, threatening, or intend to cause you harm in any way?

Harmful? Oh, no. No, no, I wouldn't use a word like harmful, and certainly not threatening. That implies some sort of... of physical danger, or malice, like she’s plotting to poison my tea or cut the brake lines on my car. It is absolutely nothing like that. My wife is not a violent or malicious person, Doctor. If anything, she’s an avoider. That is her primary psychological defense mechanism. When she is confronted with something uncomfortable, she retreats. 

So, no, she doesn't intend to cause me bodily harm. What she is doing, I believe, is trying to communicate a profound dissatisfaction—perhaps a desire to end the marriage, or maybe she wants me to figure something out so she doesn't have to be the one to initiate the confrontation. It’s a kind of emotional cowardice, really. She’s leaving these breadcrumbs, these little structural anomalies in her routine, because she can't bring herself to just sit down at the dining room table, look me in the eye, and have a difficult, adult conversation. 

The only harm being done, if you can even call it that, is to my sleep schedule and my general peace of mind. I mean, it is incredibly draining to be grading a stack of mediocre undergraduate essays on Foucault, trying to focus on postmodern power structures, while half of my brain is simultaneously trying to decipher why she suddenly started using formal punctuation in a casual text message at 5:15 PM. It elevates my blood pressure, it makes me terribly tired, and it is a massive distraction from my academic work. But do I feel threatened? Do I feel like I'm in danger? No. Not at all. I just feel like I’m trapped in this exhausting, endless game of chess where I am the only one willing to admit that we are even playing.

Have you ever had any beliefs about yourself, others, or the world that are not based in reality and persist despite clear evidence to the contrary, even outside of your concerns about your wife’s messages?

Well, I have to stop you right there, Doctor, because that phrase, not based in reality, is quite a loaded way to frame things. I mean, as a researcher, my entire professional and intellectual life is fundamentally grounded in reality. In texts, in verifiable evidence, in citations and historical context. I don't just invent concepts out of thin air. Whether I am grading a stack of freshman essays or trying to make headway on my own dissertation—which, frankly, has been stalled for months now, mostly because I simply do not have the mental bandwidth to deal with both my academic committee and my wife's behavioral anomalies—I rely strictly on what is materially presented to me. 

So, no, I do not walk around harboring wild, unfounded theories about the world or other people. I don't believe in secret societies or government conspiracies or anything absurd like that. I am a remarkably grounded, highly logical person. 

And I think that is precisely why this whole situation at home is so incredibly frustrating for me to navigate. Because people look at me, or they listen to me explain the very clear, undeniable patterns in her schedule, and they immediately want to lump me in with people who think the earth is flat. But it is not the same thing at all. My observations are entirely empirical. So aside from this situation with my wife... well, honestly, even including the situation with my wife, everything I believe is completely rooted in the factual, observable world. I just don't have the time or the inclination for things that aren't real.
Have you ever had beliefs that most people would consider completely impossible or not based in reality, even if you felt certain they were true at the time?

Doctor, I... I feel like we are just parsing semantics at this point. "Completely impossible." It’s really the exact same premise as your last question, isn't it? You’re asking if I have some sort of fundamental disconnect from reality, and I have to reiterate that my reality is entirely based on evidence. I don't do "impossible." 

Now, if you are asking whether *other* people might consider my conclusions to be impossible... well, yes, I suppose they might. Most people are, frankly, intellectually lazy. They don't look past the surface of things. Take my wife, for instance. As I keep trying to explain to you, I know she says the late meetings and the little changes in her work messages are just... well, she calls it "normal office stuff." That is her exact defense, time and time again. "Just normal office stuff, honey." And I suppose your average person, maybe even a therapist who hasn't looked at my notes, would just nod and accept that. They'd think it was completely impossible for someone to orchestrate an ongoing pattern of covert communication in their daily routine. 

But... but you have to understand, when you look at the actual timeline—and I have, I have been logging this for the past year—these things, they’ve lined up entirely too precisely to feel accidental. You don't just accidentally alter your syntax and delay your calendar updates in perfect synchronization for twelve consecutive months. It doesn't happen in a vacuum! 

So, while someone else might look at this and think it's "impossible" or absurd, I know what I'm looking at. There is a private signal in them. It is a deliberate, meticulously constructed private signal meant to tell me something she just... she won’t say directly to my face. She doesn't have the courage for a direct, adult confrontation, so she encodes it in the mundane details of her day. 

So, no, Doctor. I do not hold impossible beliefs. I just hold beliefs that require a higher level of analytical rigor than most people are willing to apply.

Have you ever had a belief about something happening or being true that you knew others could not understand, even when you tried to explain it to them, and even if it wasn’t related to your wife’s messages?

Well, again, Doctor, you're asking me to step outside of the situation with my wife, which is the only thing that's actually pertinent right now. But to answer your question... no. No, I haven't had some sort of, I don't know, esoteric revelation about the universe that I couldn't get anyone else to understand. 

I'm an academic. My entire life is about taking complex ideas—Foucault, Derrida, structuralism—and explaining them to people. Granted, trying to explain the panopticon to an eighteen-year-old who is more concerned with their fraternity rush is an exercise in futility, but that's a failure of their attention span, not a failure of reality. When I explain something, I use citations. I use historical precedent. I use logic. If someone doesn't understand me, it's usually because they haven't done the reading, not because I'm speaking in tongues or harboring some sort of secret, incomprehensible truth about the world.
